text: Ted-E-Bear taps his vest before every adventure. Tap-tap means, 'I can try.' But this morning his paw finds an empty spot. His lucky button is gone. Corgi-on-the-Cob sniffs the curling threads, then sneezes a tiny pop of corn. The first clues are waiting beside Ted's bed.

Outside, fresh paw marks cross the path. Ted's tummy feels fluttery. What if the trail is too long? Corgi presses his nose to the first print and gives a hopeful bark-pop. Ted takes one careful step, then another. Trying feels a little like courage.

Beneath the oak, numbered acorns sit in a neat row. One has rolled into the clover, leaving a gap. Corgi wants to chase it, but Ted studies the caps. 'Wait,' he says. 'The row is trying to tell us something.'

A little bridge stretches over the creek. One side has a short line of stepping planks; the other has a longer line. Ted does not like wobbling. Corgi trots onto the side with more places to step, then turns and waits. Ted touches the empty spot on his vest. 'I can still try.'

On the hill, picnic napkins flap in the breeze. Something gold flashes beneath them, then disappears. Corgi's tail starts popping so quickly that Ted laughs. Together they lift each napkin while the warm smell of honey-oat buns drifts from the basket.

The button was holding down the picnic cloth all along. Ted sews it back onto his vest, then pauses. He crossed the path, solved the acorns, and braved the bridge without it. Corgi leans close. Tap-tap. 'Lucky button,' says Ted, 'meet my brave paws.'
expected: How many loose threads curl from Ted's vest?
Two threads — and one points towards the door.
How many prints cross the path?
Four prints lead straight to the Great Oak.
Which number belongs in the gap?
Five! The runaway acorn points towards the picnic hill.
Which group has more?
5 planks
7 planks
They match
Seven steady planks carry both friends safely across.
How many napkins hid the golden glint?
Nine napkins lifted — and there is Ted's button!
Two equal groups of five make how many treats?
Two fives make ten — enough for a brave picnic together.

text: On the first day of the year, Ted-E-Bear found an empty honey jar at the back of his cupboard. He washed it, dried it and pushed a cork into the top. Then he wrote a note on a scrap of paper, folded it twice and dropped it in. "There," he said. "One good thing."

After that, whenever something good happened, Ted wrote it down. Some notes were on yellow paper, some on blue and some on the backs of old shopping lists. He never read them again. He just watched the jar fill up, a little at a time, like snow on a windowsill.

Now it was the last day of the year. The jar was so full that the cork squeaked when Ted pushed it in. Professor Hooten was having a New Year's Eve party at the library, and Ted had a plan. He tied a red ribbon round the jar's neck. "I'm going to read the whole year out loud," he told Corgi-on-the-Cob. "From the very first note to the very last."

Corgi trotted beside him all the way to the library, which was unusual. Corgi usually ran ahead. "What if it's boring?" said Ted. "A whole year is a lot of things." "It won't be boring," said Corgi. He sounded very sure about it.

The library had a separate stone step in front of the door. Tonight it wore a thin, shiny coat of ice. Ted's paws were cold. The jar was heavy. He stepped up, and his boot slid one way while the jar slid the other.

The jar landed in a soft bank of snow and didn't break. But the cork popped out, and the notes flew everywhere, like a flock of small paper birds. Some landed on the step. Some landed in the snow. One blew all the way to the gate before Corgi caught it in his mouth.

Nutmeg and Panda-Cake came running out to help. They gathered every note they could find and carried them inside in a mixing bowl. Ted looked into the bowl. His whole year was in there, all jumbled up. "I never wrote the dates," he said quietly. "Now I can't read them in order."

"Then we'll put them back in order," said Professor Hooten. "We'll be detectives. Every note will have a clue." He fetched a long piece of string and tied it between two bookcases. Then he gave Panda-Cake a box of wooden pegs.

Nutmeg cut out twelve paper squares and wrote a month on each one: January, February, March, all the way to December. Panda-Cake pegged them along the string, one month after another. "Now," said Hooten. "Read us a note, Ted. Then tell us where it goes."

Ted unfolded the first one. It was slightly damp. Corgi and I built a snow bear. It looked more like a loaf. "Snow," said Nutmeg. "So it's winter. That could be January or February." "Or December," said Panda-Cake. "It was the very first note in the jar," said Ted slowly. "I remember the loaf." He pegged it under January.

The next note was on blue paper. It rained on our picnic, so we had a puddle party instead. A duckling came. "Ducklings hatch in spring," said Nutmeg. "April, maybe. Or May." Ted pegged it under April. Then he moved it to May. Then he moved it back to April, because that was when the big puddles were.

I read the whole welcome card out loud at the picnic. Corgi helped me with the first sounds. "That was the summer picnic on the cliff," said Panda-Cake. "The day it was so hot the jam melted." Ted pegged it under July. He was beginning to enjoy this.

Eight lanterns. Two dark paths. Everyone got home. "The lantern walk," said Hooten. "It gets dark early in autumn. That was October." Found the missing button. It was under the bench all along. Nobody could remember when that one happened. Not even Ted. They pegged it in the middle of the year and decided that was good enough.

There were three December notes: a shadow show, a snowball truce and a parcel under the tree on Christmas morning. "December is getting crowded," said Nutmeg. "December is always crowded," said Hooten.

Ted picked up the next note. The writing was big and wobbly, and at the bottom there was a sandy paw print. At the sledging hill, Ted pulled my sled back up every time. Even when his legs were tired. Ted frowned. "I didn't write this one."

He unfolded another. Same wobbly writing. Same paw print. Ted carried the last parcel all the way across the hall to Moss, who had only just moved here. And another. It rained all afternoon, so Ted made his blanket fort big enough for Panda-Cake too. Even though it was only a small blanket.

Ted sorted the bowl into two piles. His own neat notes went on one side. The wobbly notes went on the other. The wobbly pile was nearly as big as his. "These aren't things that happened to me," said Ted. "They're things I did."

Everyone turned to look at Corgi. Corgi looked at the ceiling. Then at the floor. Then at the ceiling again. "You left the jar on the shelf by your door," he said at last. "And the cork isn't very tight."

"You put these in?" asked Ted. "All year?" "Only when you weren't looking," said Corgi. "You only wrote the good things that happened to you. Nobody was writing down the good things you did." Ted didn't say anything for a moment. He held the wobbly note about the sledging hill very carefully, as if it might fly away again.

"Where do Corgi's notes go?" asked Panda-Cake. That part was easy. Sledging meant snow, so that was winter. The last parcel was Christmas morning. The rainy blanket fort was spring. Soon the string was full, from January to December. Blue notes, yellow notes and wobbly notes with paw prints, all mixed together.
Ted stepped back and looked at it. It was a much longer year than he remembered. And there was much more of him in it.

Across the room, Professor Hooten's wall of clocks showed eight o'clock. In one far-away city, it was midnight already. Cluck O'Clock and Coop-Accino banged their pot lids. "Not yet, not yet… NOW!" everybody shouted. "Happy New Year, Dubai!" "Now it's your turn, Ted," said Hooten.

So Ted read the year out loud, one note at a time, from January all the way to December. When he read a neat note, everyone smiled. When he read a wobbly one, everyone looked at Corgi, and Corgi looked at the ceiling. It wasn't boring at all.

At the end, Ted took the notes off the string and put every one of them back in the honey jar. This time he pushed the cork in tightly. Then he looked at the empty string. "Next year needs a jar too," he said. "A jar each."

Hooten found four more jars in the library kitchen. One for Nutmeg. One for Panda-Cake. One for himself. And one for Corgi. Nutmeg tied a ribbon round each one, and Panda-Cake wrote their names on the lids.

Ted tore a scrap of paper from his yellow notebook. He wrote something on it, folded it twice and dropped it into Corgi's empty jar. "What does it say?" asked Corgi. "You'll find out next New Year's Eve," said Ted. It was the first good thing of the year. And it wasn't even nine o'clock.

The woodland picnic ends beneath a purple sky. Ted-E-Bear sets out 8 little lanterns for the paths, with 6 spare lanterns waiting in his wagon. One path leads to Honey-Beats's cottage and the other leads to his own. "Nobody should walk home in the dark," Ted says.
At the bend, the wind blows out 2 of Honey-Beats's 4 lanterns. Ted hears a worried little hum beyond the trees and turns back.
Two lanterns are not much, but Honey-Beats holds them high. "Small lights still count," she says. Ted moves the 2 still-glowing path lanterns to the narrow bridge, one on each side.
Three fireflies settle near each lantern. Their gold-green light makes the bridge sparkle, and Honey-Beats's shoulders finally relax.
The cottage window appears at the top of the hill. Ted still has the 6 spare lanterns in his wagon and wants both friends to carry the same number.
Honey-Beats places 3 lanterns outside. Ted places 3 inside. The cottage glows like a tiny sunrise, and the dark no longer feels so large.

Before Ted leaves, Honey-Beats gives him half of 4 honey biscuits for his walk. "You came back for me," she says. Ted smiles. "That is what friends do." They relight the path lanterns for the walk home.
expected: If Ted shares 8 lanterns equally between 2 paths, how many lanterns light each path?
A half means two equal groups. Share one lantern to each path until all 8 are used: 4 on each path.
Honey-Beats had 4 glowing lanterns and 2 went out. How many are still glowing?
Take away the 2 lanterns that went out: 4 − 2 = 2.
Ted doubles 1 lantern so both sides match. How many lanterns are there altogether?
Double 1 means 1 + 1. That makes 2.
There are 2 lanterns with 3 fireflies beside each one. How many fireflies are helping?
There are two equal groups of 3. Count 3 + 3 = 6 fireflies.
What is half of 6 lanterns?
Split 6 into two equal groups: 3 and 3. Half of 6 is 3.
What is double 3?
Double 3 is two groups of 3: 3 + 3 = 6.
How many biscuits is half of 4?
Four shared into two equal parts is 2 and 2. Half of 4 is 2.

text: Ted-E-Bear has one important job at the First Picnic: read the welcome card when the gate opens. He practised beside his bed. He practised beside the bath. But now the card trembles in his paws, and every word looks much bigger than it did at home.

Corgi-on-the-Cob sits beside Ted without telling him to hurry. His tail gives one soft bark-pop against the basket. "I cannot carry the words for you," Corgi says, "but I can listen for the first sound." Ted folds the card and puts it safely in his pocket.

They walk the quiet path before the guests arrive. Pinecones lie under the pines, and pebbles press into the mud. "Pinecone. Pine. Pebble. Path," Ted says. Four words begin with the same little puff of air. He tucks the P sound into an imaginary pocket.

At the bridge, leaves lift and land while the creek makes a low, laughing sound. Ted listens. "Leaf. Lift. Land. Low." The L sound feels smooth and light on his tongue. Into the other pocket it goes. The card no longer feels quite so heavy.

A breeze flips the picnic sign, and Ted spots a word beginning with H. He opens his mouth, but the sound is only warm air. "It is hiding," he says. Corgi shakes his head. "Not hiding. H is a soft breath, as at the start of hello. Quiet sounds still count." Ted pockets the gentle breath.

Footsteps gather beyond the gate. Ted's tummy flips. He could slip behind the bun table and nobody would be angry. Then Corgi touches the pocket holding P, and Ted touches the pocket holding L. He has not learned every word. He has learned how to begin one.

Ted unfolds the card. The first word is WELCOME. "W," he whispers. Wind. Warm. Welcome. His voice wobbles on the second word, so he stops, breathes, and begins it again. Nobody laughs. Corgi's ears point towards every sound as if each one matters-because it does.

The gate swings open. Ted reads the final line slowly, with pauses in all the right places and one pause that was not planned. Then the picnic erupts in cheers. His voice was never too small. It was exactly big enough to carry one sound, then another, all the way to the end.
Ted-E-Bear stacks his softest pillows between two chairs. He wants a reading fort big enough for one bear and one enormous adventure.
He pulls a blue blanket over the top-but whoomph! It slides down and buries him in a woolly heap.
Panda-Cake holds one corner while Ted clips the other. Inside their sturdy fort, Ted switches on a lamp and opens a story they can share.
Rain whispers at the window, but the little fort is cosy and bright. Ted decides the best forts are not the biggest-they are the ones with room for a friend.

They held and clipped the blanket together

Read a story together

text: Ten red hens sit.
A hen naps in the pen.
Nan had a red net.
Nan met ten hens.
Ten hens ran and ran!
The hens hid in the pen.
Nan sat. Nan is sad.
Ten red hens sit! Nan can nap.
A cat sat in a hat.
A rat ran at the cat.
The cat can nap. The rat can tap.
Tap, tap, tap!
The cat is mad.
The rat hid in a can.
The cat sat and sat.
The rat and the cat nap in the hat!

Christmas morning turned the library steps pink. Ted-E-Bear stamped the snow off his boots. Inside, Professor Hooten was putting an extra cup on the table. Every chair had a cup beside it already. "Who's that for?" asked Ted. "We might need it," said Hooten.

Corgi-on-the-Cob came skidding up the path with a parcel under his chin. "Did I miss the presents?" "You missed a chance to walk slowly," said Ted. Corgi shook snow out of his ears. A whole lump dropped down the back of Ted's scarf.

Panda-Cake carried in a warm jug of cocoa. Hooten pulled the chairs into a ring around the paper tree they'd made for the hall. "A little room by the door, please," Hooten said. Corgi moved his chair. Then he moved it back a tiny bit. From there he could see his parcel.

Corgi's gift from Ted was a red ball with a white stripe. Corgi rolled it along his nose and caught it under his chin. "I can do three in a row," he said. The ball rolled behind the tree on the second go.

Ted opened Corgi's gift. It was a yellow notebook with a pencil tucked through a loop. The first page was quite clean, except for one sandy paw print. "That's so you know which way up it goes," said Corgi. Ted decided to leave the print right where it was.

Panda-Cake tried on his new green oven mitts. He could pick up the warm jug with them, but he couldn't pick up a single biscuit. He held the plate for Corgi instead. When the paper had been gathered and folded, Hooten said, "That's the presents opened."

Ted bent to get the red ball from behind the tree. Something blue caught his eye under the lowest branch. It was a cord, tied around a plain brown box. A tag stuck out from the knot. "Wait," Ted said. "There's one left."

Corgi put his nose right up to the tag. Ted turned it so they could both see. It said, "For whoever gets there last." "That's me," said Corgi. "I was the last one through the door." Ted looked at the cup without a chair.

"You were the last so far," Ted said. Corgi sat down. "If someone else comes, do I give it back?" "You haven't picked it up." "Good. Then I've already given it back." He left the parcel where it was and nudged his ball over to Ted.

They rolled the ball towards the table. It stopped by the extra cup. "Maybe 'there' means here," said Corgi. "Whoever gets their cocoa last." Panda-Cake set the jug down. "That'll be me if I have to pour it for everyone first." His own cup stood empty next to the jug.

Ted turned to the first clean page of his notebook. He wrote DOOR on one line and COCOA on another. "Presents?" said Corgi. "We've all opened ours." "I know. But what if someone hasn't?" Ted wrote PRESENTS underneath. Now there were three things that "there" could mean.

Corgi went back to the tree. He held one end of the blue cord up in the light. "Look at that knot," he said. "The end goes back through twice." He pointed towards the wall. The library's noticeboard hung from a cord with the very same knot.

Ted climbed onto a low stool so he could see. Both cords had three thin white strands twisted through the blue. "Hooten keeps a whole spool of it in his drawer," he said. Just then, Hooten opened that drawer. Inside, beside the string, lay a little silver camera.

Before Ted could ask about the cord, there was a knock. Corgi rushed over. Hooten reached the door first. On the step stood a young hare in a plum coat. Her ears stuck out of a knitted hood. She held a tin against her chest.

"I'm Moss," said the hare. "We moved into the house by the bridge. The snow was up to my knees." She looked at the folded wrapping paper. "I've missed it, haven't I?" "The cocoa's warm," said Panda-Cake. "Come and show me what's in your tin."

Moss had brought ginger biscuits. Some were shaped like hares. One was shaped like half a hare. "I dropped that one," she said. "That's the one I'd choose," said Corgi. "It's already started." Moss smiled and took off her coat. Her ears sprang straight out of the hood.

Hooten poured cocoa into the extra cup. Ted fetched a chair so Moss could sit at the table. "You kept her cup ready," Ted said to Hooten. "I kept a cup ready," said Hooten. "I didn't know whose it would be." Ted thought about the box under the tree.

Ted held up his notebook. "We guessed it might mean the door. Or the cocoa. Then Corgi said the presents. Is that what 'there' means?" Hooten nodded. "I tied that parcel for whoever came after the others had opened theirs." "So there'd still be one," said Corgi.

Ted picked up the box. "Moss, I think it's yours." She tucked one long ear behind her shoulder so it wouldn't dip in her cocoa. Then she pulled the loose end of the cord. Inside the box lay a small wooden frame. There was no picture in it.

A folded note sat behind the glass. Moss read it aloud. "Choose our first Christmas morning picture." Professor Hooten brought over the silver camera. "I thought we could put up a new one every Christmas," he said. "You get to choose what goes in the first frame."

"I can take a good one," said Moss. "I take pictures of the birds by our bridge." She lifted the camera. Through it she could see a bit of the tree and most of Ted. Panda-Cake was hidden behind a chair. "We'll have to move the chairs."

Moss put the chairs near the tree. She asked Hooten to sit down and Panda-Cake to stand behind him. Ted sat on the floor. Corgi lay beside Ted with his nose on the red ball. Moss raised the camera again. There was exactly one empty chair in the picture.

"That one's for you," said Ted. "I'm usually behind the camera," Moss said. Hooten showed her a little switch. "This gives you ten seconds to get to the chair." Moss set the camera on a low wooden stool and aimed it at the tree. "I can get there in four."

Moss pressed the button and hurried over. One, two, three, four. She made it. Then Corgi tried to grin without letting go of his ball. It slipped from under his nose and bumped the stool. Click. "I think it took me jumping," said Corgi.

Hooten held out the camera. On the little screen was a crooked picture. The tree leaned sideways. Corgi was halfway out of the picture, with his tail straight up. Everyone else was laughing. Moss was right in the middle of them. "We could take another," said Hooten.

"I choose that one," said Moss. She put the empty frame on the shelf next to the tree. Ted opened his notebook and wrote the date, ready for when they printed the picture. Corgi carried his ball to the door. He waited there until everybody else had gone through.
Vincent Van Mouse had painted six chimneys, four puddles and the little bakery door. He paused over a roof that he knew by heart. His own house had just enough room for a crooked chimney and a mouse.

The picture was for the library's Christmas window. Tonight, when the snow made the streets go blue, everyone would come to see it. Vincent imagined them finding their houses. He wondered who would spot his first.

Panda-Cake brought a tin of biscuits for the audience. "There's a bit of red on your nose," he told him. Vincent rubbed his cheek. "Other side." He rubbed his chin. Panda-Cake handed him a clean rag, which he forgot to use.
Together they lifted the long painting. "I'll hold this end," said Panda-Cake. "You hold yours." Vincent trotted backwards towards the window. The picture sagged in the middle, like a washing line.
Professor Hooten opened the hall door to bring in the chairs. Cold air rushed past him. The small paper stars on the shelf trembled. Then the great sheet of painted paper gave a shiver of its own.
"Hold it there!" cried Vincent. He gripped his end with both paws. Panda-Cake held his. The gust pushed the middle up and over the corner of the window latch.
Rrrrip. A rip ran down the Christmas street, stopping just above the bottom edge. Half of Vincent's chimney folded back. He could see Panda-Cake through the hole where his house ought to have been.

Hooten shut the door. "That was a big gust," he said softly. Vincent put the painting on the table. He tried to press the chimney flat. His paw was shaking, so Panda-Cake set the rag beside him and waited.

They tried to mend the rip from behind. The two sides almost met. But the paint had stuck to the latch and come away, leaving a white stripe down the wall of Vincent's house. He tucked his brush inside his apron.
Outside, one child stood on tiptoe to peer through the glass. Another was brushing snow off the window ledge with a mitten. Vincent could see them. He slid down in his chair so they couldn't see him.
Panda-Cake took a cardboard star from the shelf. "We could put a star over the white bit." The desk lamp was already on. When he picked up the star, its shadow swept over the wall.
"Hold it there," said Vincent. This time he said it very quietly. He watched the star grow when Panda-Cake moved it towards the lamp. When he moved back, it shrank. He climbed out of his chair.
Vincent snipped round the torn flap and lifted it. On the wall, the scrap became a steep little roof. He tipped it sideways, and there was his crooked chimney. "There you are," he said.

"Hooten, may we borrow a sheet?" asked Vincent. "And could the chairs face this way?" He pointed away from the window, towards the warm end of the hall, where two low bookcases stood with a gap between them.

Hooten clipped a plain sheet to two tall poles behind the bookcases and set the lamp on a table behind it. Panda-Cake walked round to the front. Vincent lifted his roof. A house popped up on the sheet. "I can see it from here!" he called.
Vincent took his little scissors. From the snowy strip below the rip, he snipped a new row of roofs. Panda-Cake cut a cardboard squirrel with a parcel under its arm.

The squirrel looked very fine from the front, until Panda-Cake tried to make it walk. Its parcel bumped a roof. Its tail went up a chimney. "That's the wrong way home," said Vincent, laughing for the first time since the rip.

They tried again. This time the squirrel stood farther from the lamp, beside the sheet. Small enough! It trotted down the street between the roofs. Vincent practised making the star rise. Panda-Cake practised three little taps.

Hooten went out to the waiting children. "The Christmas picture is ready," he said. "Come inside and find a chair." Behind the sheet, Vincent heard boots tapping and two last chairs scraping along the floor.
Panda-Cake tapped his spoon on the biscuit tin. Ting. Ting. Ting. The hall went quiet. Vincent raised the little street. On the sheet, rooftops grew out of a pool of gold.
A squirrel travelled from house to house. At the last door, she set down her parcel and knocked. Then up came the star. A small voice in the front row whispered, "That's Vincent's chimney."

Vincent almost forgot to move the star. He had thought his chimney was ruined. Here it was, as crooked as ever, big enough for the whole room to see. He held the star steady while the audience clapped.

Afterwards the children took turns with the puppets. One made the squirrel as big as a house. One put the star in the squirrel's paws. Panda-Cake opened the biscuit tin. Vincent looked down and found another red spot on his apron.

He turned off the lamp and carried the crooked little house to the window. Outside, the snow had stopped. The silhouette sat on the sill beside the last biscuit. Vincent licked a crumb off his paw. "Good night, little house."

The town square has one long blank wall, and the Harvest Festival is in three days. Vincent Van Mouse unrolls his sketch: a sunset over the hills, small enough to fit in his paw. "Every centimetre on my sketch becomes 25 centimetres on the wall," he explains. Stripe-Scout whistles. Sail-Affe stretches her neck to see the top of the wall.
Vincent's sunset orange is always mixed from red and yellow in the ratio 2:3. Stripe-Scout has already poured 8 pots of red into the big mixing tub and is waiting, brush ready, for the yellow.

On the second morning, Stripe-Scout finds yesterday's tub. Its label says 10 pots of red to 15 pots of yellow. Her ears flatten. "I mixed it wrong. It's ruined." Vincent doesn't answer straight away. He simplifies the ratio first, the way a careful artist checks a colour before judging it.

Vincent chalks a grid of 45 squares onto the wall. Sail-Affe can reach the high squares without a ladder, and Stripe-Scout is quickest along the bottom. They agree to split the squares in the ratio 4:5, high to low.

On the last afternoon, grey clouds roll over the hills. Seven squares are still bare. Stripe-Scout wants to give up and throw a sheet over the wall, but Vincent checks the clock instead. They have been painting 3 squares every 12 minutes, steady and neat.

They finish with minutes to spare, and the first raindrops miss the wall. One small pot of gold paint is left for the sun's rays. Vincent shares its 30 ml in the ratio 1:2:3 between himself, Sail-Affe and Stripe-Scout, because Stripe-Scout has the most rays to paint.

At the festival, the whole town gathers in front of the wall. The sunset glows exactly like the sketch, only twenty-five times taller. Professor Hooten asks for a postcard of the mural for every reader in the library. Vincent smiles. Scaling works in both directions.
expected: The sketch is 8 cm tall. If every 1 cm becomes 25 cm, how tall will the mural be, in centimetres?
Scaling multiplies every length by the same factor: 8 × 25 = 200 cm. Adding 25 instead (8 + 25 = 33) would squash the picture out of proportion.
Red and yellow are mixed in the ratio 2:3. There are 8 pots of red. How many pots of yellow are needed?
2 parts are 8 pots, so 1 part is 4 pots. Yellow is 3 parts: 3 × 4 = 12. Keeping the same difference instead (8 + 1 = 9) would change the colour.
Simplify 10:15 so that the first number is 2. What is the second number?
Divide both parts by 5: 10 ÷ 5 = 2 and 15 ÷ 5 = 3, so 10:15 is 2:3, the very same orange. Taking 8 away from both parts (2:7) does not keep the ratio.
45 squares are shared in the ratio 4:5. How many squares does Sail-Affe paint?
4 + 5 = 9 parts altogether. 45 ÷ 9 = 5 squares in each part. Sail-Affe paints 4 parts: 4 × 5 = 20.
At the same rate, how many minutes will 7 squares take?
Find the time for one square first: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 minutes. Then 7 × 4 = 28 minutes. Adding 4 more minutes (12 + 4 = 16) treats a proportion as an addition.
30 ml is shared in the ratio 1:2:3. How many millilitres does Stripe-Scout get?
1 + 2 + 3 = 6 parts. 30 ÷ 6 = 5 ml in each part. Stripe-Scout has 3 parts: 3 × 5 = 15 ml.
The mural is 200 cm tall. At a scale of 1 to 25, how tall is the postcard picture, in centimetres?
To scale down, divide every length by 25: 200 ÷ 25 = 8 cm. That is exactly the size of Vincent's first sketch.

text: Wise Owl hangs 24 lantern flags for the reading festival. Booklava tries one long row, but the tall gateposts hide half the display. Quill-Berry suggests testing equal rectangles until every visitor can see.

Four boxes of chimes are labelled 21, 23, 25 and 27. Booklava wants to hang each box in equal rows, with more than one row and more than one chime in every row. One box will not share out that way: its chimes only hang as one long row. That box holds a prime number of chimes.
Booklava ties a purple ribbon every fourth flag. Quill-Berry ties a gold ribbon every sixth flag. Wise Owl asks them to find the first place after the starting post where both colours will meet.

For the centre of the festival, 16 purple and gold cushions must form a perfect square, with clear paths on every side. Booklava smiles: the earlier rectangles were not mistakes, just different factor pairs. The final festival celebrates every elegant solution.
expected: If the 24 flags hang in 4 equal rows, how many flags go in each row?
Four rows of 6 make 4 × 6 = 24. So 4 and 6 are a factor pair of 24.
Which number is prime?
Twenty-three has exactly two factors, 1 and 23, so its chimes only make 1 row of 23. The others can be shared out: 21 = 3 × 7, 25 = 5 × 5 and 27 = 3 × 9.
What is the first common multiple of 4 and 6 after zero?
Multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12... and multiples of 6 are 6, 12... The first match is 12.
How many cushions belong in each row of a square made from 16 cushions?
A square has the same number of rows and columns. Since 4 × 4 = 16, each row has 4 cushions. That makes 16 a square number.

text: Wise Owl opens the library and finds Quill-Berry waiting outside with a folded page. "I wrote something," Quill whispers, "but I am not sure I can share it."
A gust slips through the door and carries the poem beneath a table. Quill-Berry freezes, certain everyone will laugh if they read it.
Meow-inara finds the page but does not read it. She returns it in the quiet corner and asks, "Would you like one friendly listener?"
Quill-Berry reads her poem to two friends, then four, then the whole afternoon circle. Wise Owl adds a blank page to the display for whatever Quill writes next.
expected: Why did returning the poem unread help Quill-Berry?
It let Quill choose when and with whom to share
Meow-inara respected Quill and offered one friendly listener.
What carried the poem beneath the table?
A gust of wind
